newsitem.title: EGYPT: Sudanese rebels say advance, government mobilises.
newsitem.headline: Sudanese rebels say advance, government mobilises.

text.p: Sudanese rebels said on Wednesday they had captured or attacked more army garrisons in the east of Sudan and were advancing on the southern Blue Nile town of Damazin.

Sudanese President Omar Hassan al-Bashir said the gun would decide the struggle for power in Africa's largest country and his vice president flew to Cairo in what the opposition said was another sign of panic in government circles.

Bashir turned to Islamic rhetoric to muster recruits to drive back the rebels, who are comprised of northerners and southerners working together in their first combined offensive to overthrow the Islamist government that took power in a military coup in 1989.

In the Eritrean capital Asmara, a spokesman for the rebel Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA) said the rebels were within 80 km (50 miles) of Damazin, site of a hydroelectricity plant that provides 80 percent of the capital Khartoum's power.

A joint rebel force, combining elements of the southern SPLA and the mainly northern Sudan Alliance Forces, on Tuesday captured the garrison at Gadamyeeb, northeast of Kassala town, and were attacking nearby garrisons, the SPLA added.

The attacks in the Kassala area, east of the capital Khartoum, add a third area of operations to the rebel offensive. They previously had reported military successes on two stretches of the Ethiopian border -- at the town of Kurmuk in Blue Nile province and in another area just north of the Blue Nile river.
The rebels say their objective is not to capture the capital but to squeeze the government and ignite a popular uprising.
One SPLA spokesman, Yasser Arman, said the latest rebel advance was a turning point in 13 years of war against Khartoum.

"This operation is to enable the mass movement inside Sudan to wage an uprising against the military junta there. By advancing on Damazin we are piling economic and military pressure on the junta," Arman said.
In Khartoum, President Bashir added his voice to the government's campaign to prepare public opinion for war, using the terminology of jihad (holy war).
He again blamed the attacks on Ethiopian forces, demoting the rebels to the status of junior partners.

"Scores of mujahidin (jihad fighters) are now hurrying towards the theatre of operation in order to defend the eastern front and teach the aggressors and the traitors a lesson they will never forget," Sudanese radio quoted Bashir as saying. he radio was monitored by the British Broadcasting Corporation.
"Bashir said political and diplomatic channels (to Ethiopia) had been closed. He said the only thing left now was the power of the gun," the radio added.
Ethiopia says it has nothing to do with the attacks and that Khartoum is looking for a scapegoat for its internal problems.
Bashir's first vice president, Major-General al-Zubeir Mohammad Saleh, arrived in Cairo unexpectedly on Wednesday on a mission cloaked in some secrecy.
One official said Saleh went to the offices of President Hosni Mubarak. But presidency sources said Mubarak had no appointments on Wednesday morning and the press was not invited.
Saleh is the most senior Sudanese to visit Egypt since President Omar Hassan al-Bashir came in June for an Arab summit.
Relations have been extremely bad for years, especially since Egypt said Sudan helped the Egyptian Islamists who tried to kill Mubarak in Addis Ababa in 1995. Sudan denies this.
Two of Sudan's neighbours, Eritrea and Uganda, have broken relations with Khartoum but Egypt has refused to follow suit, arguing that this would damage the Sudanese people.
Egypt also has an uneasy relationship with some of the opposition groups fighting the Khartoum government.
In Cairo, opposition spokesman Farouq Abu Eissa told Reuters Saleh's visit was another sign that Khartoum was desperate.
"They are in panic. It's clear that they are isolated. There was a very small turnout at the demonstrations they tried to organise in Khartoum yesterday," he added.
Abu Eissa said the leadership of the National Democratic Alliance, the umbrella opposition organisation, met in Cairo on Tuesday and was about to make a formal appeal for an uprising.
"We call on people inside Sudan to organise their uprising. We call on military personnel to unite and join our forces and make the uprising, protected by the gun, a reality," he said.
"We call on the army to distance itself from the NIF (National Islamic Front) regime, which has humiliated our people," he added.
